value.overview: The Gray-cowled Wood-Rail (Aramides cajaneus) is a secretive, chicken-sized rail of Central and South America. It spends much of its time walking through dense vegetation rather than flying, and it is often detected by its loud, repeated calls. The species is associated with wet forests, forest edges, river margins, swamps, mangroves, and other areas with thick ground cover. It can also use disturbed habitats when suitable cover and moisture remain available.
value.classification: The Gray-cowled Wood-Rail belongs to the rail family, Rallidae, and the genus Aramides. Taxonomic treatment of wood-rails has changed, and some older sources use the name Gray-necked Wood-Rail for this species or for a broader former species concept.
value.identification: This medium-sized rail has a gray head and neck, an olive-brown to greenish back, a rich chestnut breast and upper flanks, and strongly barred black-and-white lower flanks. The bill is yellowish to greenish with a darker tip, the eyes are reddish, and the legs are pinkish or red. It has a short tail and a laterally compressed body suited to moving through dense vegetation. In Costa Rica, careful attention to voice and range may be needed because related wood-rail forms can be difficult to separate visually.
value.rangeHabitat: The Gray-cowled Wood-Rail ranges from southern Costa Rica through Panama and much of South America east of the Andes, reaching northern Argentina and Uruguay. In Costa Rica, the species is reliably associated especially with the southern part of the country, including humid lowlands and foothill regions; taxonomic boundaries with the Russet-naped Wood-Rail are complicated in parts of Costa Rica, so regional records may sometimes be reported under a combined or differing treatment. It uses wet forest, mangroves, swamps, river margins, marsh edges, and dense secondary vegetation from lowlands into foothills.
value.migrationStatus: Generally resident. In Costa Rica, it is treated as a resident breeding species rather than a regular long-distance migrant, although local movements may occur when water levels, food, or habitat conditions change.
value.breeding: Breeding has been documented in Costa Rica from approximately April through September, although timing can vary by locality and weather. The nest is usually placed in dense vegetation near the ground or above wet ground, and both adults participate in incubation and care of the young. Clutches commonly contain several pale eggs marked with brown. The chicks are precocial and leave the nest soon after hatching while remaining under parental care.
value.dietFeeding: The Gray-cowled Wood-Rail forages mainly on the ground, walking slowly through leaf litter, muddy margins, dense vegetation, and shallow wet areas. Its diet includes insects and other invertebrates, small aquatic animals, seeds, fruits, and occasionally other small food items. It probes and turns through debris with its bill and may feed along streams, marsh edges, mangroves, and forest clearings, often where moist soil makes prey easier to find.
value.behavior: This rail is usually shy and spends much of the day concealed in thick vegetation, but it may walk into open areas such as lawns, paths, gardens, or stream margins where cover is nearby. It is more often heard than seen. Its loud, rhythmic calls may be given by pairs or neighboring birds and can carry through forest. It is a strong runner and generally flies only short distances when flushed or crossing gaps.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not clearly quantified, and available assessments do not indicate a level of decline that meets a threatened-category threshold.
